title: 1955 Altensteig mid-air collision
summary: Formation of nine military transport aircraft conducting training mission just after takeoff from Stuttgart-Echterdingen. One aircraft on right of formation of three at 4000 feet altitude developed engine problems. After losing height the aircraft climbed abruptly colliding in mid-air with second aircraft of formation. First aircraft serial number 53-7841 with 19 occupants disintegrated and crashed immediately. Second aircraft 53-3222 with 47 occupants continued in flight before crashing in wooded area 30 miles from Stuttgart. All 66 personnel killed making it deadliest air crash in Germany at that time.
probable_cause: Engine failure on leading aircraft resulted in loss and abrupt recovery that led to mid-air collision with formation mate.

factors.evidence: one aircraft on right of formation developed engine problems just after takeoff when it was around 4000 feet
the aircraft lost height then climbed abruptly into the second aircraft
two aircraft collided in mid-air three miles from Altensteig
both aircraft burst into flames after crashing

events.text: Just after 14:00 during takeoff one aircraft on the right of a formation of three developed engine problems when it was around 4000 feet altitude.
The aircraft with engine problems lost height then climbed abruptly.
The first aircraft collided in mid-air with the second aircraft of the formation three miles from Altensteig.

The first aircraft serial number 53-7841 crashed and disintegrated with the loss of all 19 on board while the second aircraft 53-3222 crashed 30 miles from Stuttgart in a wooded area and burst into flames killing all 47 on board.

notes: text states formation flying but does not provide engine failure investigation details
deadliest aviation accident in Germany at time of occurrence

title: United Airlines 409
summary: United Airlines Flight 409, a Douglas DC-4 carrying 66 people, crashed into Medicine Bow Peak near Laramie, Wyoming on October 6, 1955 while cruising at its assigned altitude of 10,000 feet. The wreckage showed the aircraft in a nose-up attitude at low airspeed, indicating the crew was attempting to climb. The CAB investigation identified three possible contributing factors: inaccurate altimeter reading, cloud obscuration of the mountain peak, or downdrafts around the peak.
probable_cause: Exact cause could not be determined. Possible contributing factors included altimeter malfunction causing incorrect altitude indication, cloud obscuration preventing visual detection of terrain, or downdrafts pushing the aircraft toward the mountain.

factors.evidence: Mountain obscuration by clouds prevented visual sighting of the mountain peak before it was too late to react.
Inaccurate altimeter indicating altitude could have led pilot to believe aircraft was higher than actual position.
Turbulence, specifically downdrafts around Medicine Bow peak, may have pushed Flight 409 into the mountain.
Wreckage study suggested nose up attitude and unusually low airspeed, implying aircraft was attempting climb at time of crash.
Aircraft crashed into Medicine Bow Peak at 12,005 feet while in nose-up attitude.

events.text: Flight 409 departed Denver at 6:33 a.m., 83 minutes behind schedule, assigned to airway V-4 toward Laramie at 10,000 feet.
Expected position report from Rock River at 8:11 a.m. was not received; repeated attempts to contact flight were met with no response.
With airliner's status unknown, Civil Aeronautics Authority was alerted to the missing aircraft with no radar traces in the region.
Search aircraft spotted wreckage southwest of Medicine Bow Peak at 11:40 a.m. with black stain and debris visible in steep ravine.

notes: three theories presented but not definitively proven

title: United Airlines 629
summary: A dynamite bomb placed in checked luggage by John Gilbert Graham detonated at 7:03 p.m. local time while the Douglas DC-6B was cruising at altitude over Weld County, Colorado, destroying the aircraft completely. All 39 passengers and 5 crew members died in the explosion and subsequent crash. Graham had hidden the bomb in his mother's luggage to kill her for a life insurance payout. Extensive in-air breakup scattered debris across 6 square miles with major portions of wings and engines found in two craters 150 feet apart.
probable_cause: A dynamite bomb placed in the aircraft's luggage compartment by passenger John Gilbert Graham detonated during flight, destroying the aircraft. Graham acted in revenge against his mother and to obtain a large life insurance payout.

factors.evidence: a dynamite bomb placed in the checked luggage
Two bright lights suddenly appeared in the sky north-northwest of the airport, observed for 30-45 seconds before falling to the ground
Extensive in-air breakup of the entire aircraft occurred with major portions of wings, engines and center sections found in two craters
The large load of fuel ignited on impact, and the fires were so intense that despite efforts to extinguish them they continued to burn for three days

events.text: Flight 629 took off from Denver at 6:52 p.m. bound for Portland and Seattle
At 6:56 p.m. the aircraft made its last transmission, stating it was passing the Denver omni
Two bright lights suddenly appeared in the sky north-northwest of the airport at 7:03 p.m. local time, observed for 30-45 seconds before falling to the ground at roughly the same speed
Farmers and residents near Longmont reported loud explosions and fiery debris falling from the night sky

Ground searchers determined that all 44 people aboard the DC-6B had been killed; debris was scattered across 6 square miles of Weld County with major portions of wings, engines and center sections found in two craters 150 feet apart
